frameworks.name: Maker vs. Manager Time Blocking
frameworks.definition: A time-management discipline where founders explicitly declare whether each time block is dedicated to maker mode (deep work) or manager mode (meetings/decisions), then protect each block accordingly.

claims.text: A founder should personally manage their own calendar/time allocation decisions, not delegate this to an assistant, because time is the founder's most valuable resource and only the founder should decide how it is spent.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: does not apply to operational blocking/tackling execution (that can be delegated)
does not apply after founder has built replacement decision-making infrastructure

claims.text: Executive assistant hiring requires prioritizing general intelligence and response speed above other criteria: the EA should respond to all messages within 60 seconds and have sufficient horsepower to complete first drafts of complex work that the founder can then refine from 80% completion.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: High intelligence allows founder to trust EA decision-making on discretionary tasks; fast response ensures EA availability becomes the non-constraint when founder needs them

anchors.value: 80% complete first drafts that require founder refinement

bounded_by: requires EA to have general horsepower/intelligence (not just administrative skill)
requires founder to have clear maker vs manager distinction in their work

claims.text: Most founders underinvest in executive assistant compensation; the market rate is higher than founders expect because high-performing EAs are rare and generate disproportionate founder productivity returns.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder experiencing time constraint as binding bottleneck

claims.text: When a founder has properly managed maker vs. manager time blocks and has an EA tracking ongoing projects and closure loops, the founder experiences a shift from reactive firefighting to proactive work: they feel ahead of their workload rather than perpetually behind.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has designated maker mode time blocks
founder has designated manager mode time blocks
EA actively tracks closure loops and project status
claims.mechanism: Time blocking removes ambiguity about work mode; EA closure-loop tracking surfaces forgotten commitments; together these eliminate decision lag and context switching

claims.text: General intelligence in an executive assistant is more valuable than it appears: it enables the founder to delegate first-draft completion and trust the result (achieving 80% quality without founder rework), rather than forcing the founder to do all work from scratch.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: EA role requires discretionary task completion
claims.mechanism: High intelligence in EA allows them to understand task intent and fill gaps independently, reducing founder rework cycles and compounding time freed
bounded_by: does not apply to purely administrative/operational tasks where intelligence matters less

claims.text: A founder should watch the maker vs. manager framework video before hiring or onboarding an executive assistant, so the EA understands the founder's work rhythm and scheduling needs.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder operates on maker vs manager cadence

examples.text: Alex Hormozi's experience with a high-performing EA: After hiring an EA with both high intelligence and strict response-speed discipline (60-second response window), Hormozi experienced multiple productivity shifts. First, he became able to delegate first-draft task completion and trust the quality (achieving 80% rather than requiring 100% founder rework). Second, with the EA actively managing his project closure loops and reminding him of pending follow-ups, he felt proactively ahead of his workload for the first time in years, rather than constantly firefighting. This came from explicit time blocking of his maker mode and manager mode, with the EA maintaining visibility into ongoing projects and their status.

practices.text: When hiring an executive assistant, pay more than you initially expect and look specifically for high general intelligence and non-negotiable speed (60-second response time).

As a founder, explicitly time block your calendar into maker mode blocks (deep work) and manager mode blocks (decisions/meetings), then live and die by that schedule, leveraging your EA to protect the blocks.

Have your executive assistant actively track all your ongoing projects and their closure loops, regularly surfacing unresolved commitments and follow-ups so you remain proactively on top of your work.
